underreported.why_unreported: The trace-back process has operated behind the scenes since the TRACED Act took effect. Explicitly asking whether to make trace-back results public would materially shift the transparency baseline. The bill hides this study inside a 17-topic list.

underreported.summary: One consideration for exempting a provider from the Robocall Mitigation Database bond requirement is whether the provider is an issuer whose securities are listed on a national securities exchange.
underreported.why_unreported: The Robocall Mitigation Database certifications are a compliance touchpoint for all voice service providers. Building a de facto public-company exemption into the bond regime is a structural favor to large listed providers that isn't reflected in the bill's short title.

gaps: The bill directs the FCC to stand up an interagency taskforce but does not authorize appropriations or require dedicated staffing — funding is limited to existing FCC, FTC, and DOJ resources.
The bill grants the registered TRACED Act consortium trace-back immunity but does not identify remedies for parties whose call records or identifying information are shared or published in error.
The bill lets the FCC or the consortium publish a list of voice service providers but does not specify due process protections (notice, appeal, correction) for listed providers.
The bill caps the Robocall Mitigation Database bond at $100,000 but does not set a floor, leaving the effective bond amount to FCC rulemaking discretion.

added: New FCC interagency taskforce on unlawful robocalls (270-day standup deadline; 360-day report; taskforce terminates 90 days after report submission)
New Section 13(d)(3) of Public Law 116-105 (Pallone-Thune TRACED Act) — Trace-back immunity for the registered consortium
New FCC rules requirement: bond of up to $100,000 before filing certifications in the Robocall Mitigation Database, with an exempted-providers criteria framework
modified: Section 13(d)(2) of Public Law 116-105 (Pallone-Thune TRACED Act) — FCC notice provision changed from "annually" to "once every 3 years"

Section 13(e) of Public Law 116-105 (Pallone-Thune TRACED Act) — Public-list authority rewritten so FCC or consortium may publish a list based on refusal to participate in trace-back or on data about providers found to originate/transmit substantial unlawful robocalls; Commission may take enforcement action based on the information

title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
official_title: To amend title 11, United States Code, to modify certain bankruptcy eligibility requirements, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA), Chair of Senate Judiciary, with 5 cosponsors, this bill sets new debt limits for two bankruptcy tracks: $7.5 million for Subchapter V small-business reorganization and $2.75 million for Chapter 13 individual reorganization. The bill passed the Senate on August 3, 2026 and awaits House action. Similar temporary Subchapter V threshold increases (the pandemic-era CARES Act and Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment and Technical Corrections Act of 2022) have moved through both chambers on bipartisan Judiciary support, which favors House action here.

referencedSources.label: 11 U.S.C. 1182 (Bankruptcy Code — Subchapter V debtor definitions)
11 U.S.C. 109 (Bankruptcy Code — Who may be a debtor)

summary: This bill rewrites two bankruptcy debt-limit rules in title 11 of the U.S. Code. First, it replaces the current definition of "debtor" in Section 1182(1) — the eligibility gate for Subchapter V small business reorganization under Chapter 11 — with a new definition covering a person engaged in commercial or business activities (with affiliates counted together and single-asset real estate excluded) that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts of not more than $7,500,000 (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders), at least 50 percent of which arose from commercial or business activities. It bars public reporting companies and their affiliates from Subchapter V and disallows any group of affiliated debtors whose combined qualifying debts exceed $7,500,000. Second, it rewrites Section 109(e) so that only individuals with regular income (or such an individual and spouse, other than a stockbroker or commodity broker) with noncontingent liquidated debts under $2,750,000 may be a Chapter 13 debtor — replacing the current split limits for secured and unsecured debt. The amendments apply to cases commenced on or after enactment.
brief: Rewrites Subchapter V small business bankruptcy eligibility to a single $7,500,000 combined-debt limit and Chapter 13 individual eligibility to a single $2,750,000 combined-debt limit, effective for cases filed on or after enactment.

top_lines.headline: Subchapter V Small Business Debt Limit
subs: New 11 U.S.C. §1182(1)(A) covers persons engaged in commercial/business activities (including affiliates that are also debtors) with aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts of not more than $7,500,000 (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders)
At least 50 percent of the debt must have arisen from the commercial or business activities of the debtor
Excludes single-asset real estate debtors whose primary activity is owning single-asset real estate

top_lines.headline: Subchapter V Group and Public-Company Exclusions
subs: Bars any member of a group of affiliated debtors whose aggregate qualifying debts exceed $7,500,000 (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders)
Bars any debtor that is a corporation subject to Section 13 or 15(d) reporting under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78m, 78o(d))
Bars any debtor that is an affiliate of such a public reporting company

top_lines.headline: Chapter 13 Individual Debt Limit
subs: New 11 U.S.C. §109(e): only an individual with regular income (or such an individual and spouse, other than a stockbroker or commodity broker) with noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2,750,000 may be a Chapter 13 debtor
Replaces the current version of §109(e), which splits its debt limit into a secured-debt cap and an unsecured-debt cap

top_lines.headline: Effective Date
subs: The amendments made by the Act apply to any case commenced under title 11, United States Code, on or after the date of enactment

sections.label: Section 2(a) — Subchapter V Small Business Debt Limit (11 U.S.C. §1182(1))

items.main: Rewrites the definition of "debtor" for Subchapter V of Chapter 11 (Small Business Debtor Reorganization).
items.detail: The new definition is set out as a two-part structure. Subparagraph (A) covers a person engaged in commercial or business activities (including any affiliate of such person that is also a debtor under title 11, and excluding a person whose primary activity is the business of owning single-asset real estate) that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts, as of the date of the filing of the petition or the date of the order for relief, of not more than $7,500,000 (excluding debts owed to one or more affiliates or insiders), not less than 50 percent of which arose from the commercial or business activities of the debtor.

items.main: Adds three Subchapter V exclusions in new §1182(1)(B).
items.detail: The new subparagraph excludes: (i) any member of a group of affiliated debtors under title 11 that has aggregate noncontingent liquidated secured and unsecured debts greater than $7,500,000 (excluding debt owed to affiliates or insiders); (ii) any debtor that is a corporation subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. §78m, §78o(d)); and (iii) any debtor that is an affiliate of a corporation described in clause (ii).

sections.label: Section 2(b) — Chapter 13 Individual Debt Limit (11 U.S.C. §109(e))

items.main: Strikes and rewrites §109(e) so Chapter 13 eligibility is set by a single combined-debt cap.
items.detail: The new §109(e) provides: only an individual with regular income that owes, on the date of the filing of the petition, noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2,750,000 — or an individual with regular income and such individual's spouse, except a stockbroker or commodity broker, that owe, on the date of the filing of the petition, noncontingent, liquidated debts that aggregate less than $2,750,000 — may be a debtor under Chapter 13. Per the fetched text of the current 11 U.S.C. §109, this replaces a split limit that used a secured-debt cap and an unsecured-debt cap; the bill collapses that structure into a single aggregate-debt threshold.

items.main: Applies the amendments to any case commenced under title 11 on or after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Pending cases filed before enactment remain governed by prior law.

underreported.summary: The affiliated-group cap treats any member of an affiliated-debtor group whose combined qualifying debts exceed $7,500,000 as ineligible for Subchapter V — even if that member alone would qualify.
underreported.why_unreported: Coverage of Subchapter V threshold bills tends to focus on the headline dollar limit. The affiliated-group aggregation rule is the operative provision that determines how the limit applies to holding-company structures and franchisee networks.

underreported.summary: Public reporting companies (§13 or §15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act) and their affiliates are barred from Subchapter V.
underreported.why_unreported: The Subchapter V regime is generally understood to be for small businesses. Codifying a categorical exclusion for reporting companies and their affiliates puts a bright-line rule into statute that closes a workaround for public-company subsidiaries.

gaps: The bill sets a $7.5M debt cap for Subchapter V and a $2.75M debt cap for Chapter 13 but does not index either threshold to inflation, so real-terms limits will erode over time.
The bill excludes public reporting companies and their affiliates from Subchapter V but does not address privately-held companies whose beneficial owners are public reporting entities.
The bill replaces the split secured/unsecured Chapter 13 debt limit with a single aggregate cap but does not address how debts secured by a spouse's separate property are counted.
The bill applies only to cases commenced on or after enactment and does not offer transition relief for cases already dismissed on eligibility grounds under the prior thresholds.

added: New categorical exclusions from Subchapter V for members of affiliated-debtor groups over $7.5M, public reporting companies under §13 or §15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and affiliates of such reporting companies (new 11 U.S.C. §1182(1)(B))
modified: 11 U.S.C. §1182(1) — Definition of "debtor" for Subchapter V rewritten to a $7,500,000 combined-debt cap with a 50%-commercial-origin requirement
11 U.S.C. §109(e) — Chapter 13 eligibility rewritten to a single $2,750,000 aggregate noncontingent-liquidated-debt cap

title: Youth Poisoning Protection Act
official_title: To ban the sale of products with a high concentration of sodium nitrite to individuals, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) with 3 cosponsors, this bill classifies any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite (10 percent or more by weight) as a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act. The bill passed the Senate on August 3, 2026 and awaits House action. Narrow consumer-safety bans on youth-targeted poisonings typically clear both chambers when the sponsor coalition includes both parties — this bill's short length and the industrial/food-industry carveouts favor movement.
summary: This bill treats any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite (defined as 10 percent or more by weight) as a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057). A rule of construction limits the ban's reach: it does not prohibit commercial or industrial uses where high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale or use, and it does not apply to substances meeting the definition of a drug, device, cosmetic, or food under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act — including poultry and poultry products, meat and meat food products, and eggs and egg products under the Poultry Products Inspection Act, Federal Meat Inspection Act, and Egg Products Inspection Act. "Consumer product" carries its Section 3(a)(5) meaning. The ban takes effect 90 days after enactment.
brief: Classifies consumer products containing 10% or more by weight of sodium nitrite as banned hazardous products under the Consumer Product Safety Act, with commercial/industrial and food/drug carveouts, effective 90 days after enactment.

top_lines.headline: New Consumer Ban
subs: Any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite is considered a banned hazardous product
Banning authority is Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057)

top_lines.headline: "High Concentration" Defined
subs: 10 percent or more by weight of sodium nitrite

top_lines.headline: Commercial and Food-Industry Carveouts
subs: Rule of construction: does not prohibit any commercial or industrial purpose in which high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for sale to, use by, consumption by, or enjoyment of a consumer
Does not apply to substances meeting the FD&C Act definitions of drug, device, cosmetic, or food

Food carveout expressly covers poultry and poultry products, meat and meat food products, and eggs and egg products under the Poultry Products Inspection Act, Federal Meat Inspection Act, and Egg Products Inspection Act

top_lines.headline: Effective Date
subs: Takes effect 90 days after the date of enactment

items.main: Any consumer product containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite is considered a banned hazardous product under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057).
items.detail: This route uses the CPSA's existing banned-hazardous-product framework rather than creating a new regulatory regime. The Consumer Product Safety Commission's enforcement authorities under the CPSA apply.

items.main: The ban is limited to consumer-facing sales and does not reach commercial or industrial uses where high-concentration sodium nitrite is not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale, use, consumption, or enjoyment.
items.detail: This preserves industrial uses of sodium nitrite (metal treatment, laboratory reagents, corrosion inhibition, etc.) that do not touch the retail consumer channel.

items.main: The ban does not apply to substances meeting the FD&C Act definitions of drug, device, cosmetic, or food.
items.detail: Definitions cross-reference sections 201(g), (h), (i), and (f) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. §321(g), (h), (i), and (f)). The food carveout expressly includes poultry and poultry products (as defined in sections 4(e) and (f) of the Poultry Products Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §453(e) and (f))), meat and meat food products (as defined in section 1(j) of the Federal Meat Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §601(j))), and eggs and egg products (as defined in section 4 of the Egg Products Inspection Act (21 U.S.C. §1033)).

items.main: "Consumer product" carries its Section 3(a)(5) meaning under the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2052(a)(5)).
items.detail: This anchors the ban to the existing statutory definition rather than creating a bespoke one.

items.main: "High concentration of sodium nitrite" is defined as 10 percent or more by weight of sodium nitrite.
items.detail: Products below the 10% threshold — the concentration typically found in curing salts and industrial pre-mixes — are outside the ban.

items.main: Section 2 takes effect 90 days after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Retailers, distributors, and manufacturers of consumer-facing high-concentration sodium nitrite products have 90 days to clear inventory or reformulate.

underreported.summary: The commercial/industrial carveout preserves all uses of high-concentration sodium nitrite that are not customarily produced or distributed for consumer sale — leaving unrestricted a large industrial market for metal treatment, laboratory reagents, and corrosion inhibition.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's short title emphasizes youth poisoning protection, but the practical scope of the ban is set almost entirely by this carveout. Any product marketed to industrial buyers rather than end consumers stays legal, and the CPSC's enforcement calls will hinge on whether a product is "customarily" distributed to consumers.

gaps: The bill bans consumer products containing 10 percent or more sodium nitrite but does not address online marketplace enforcement, cross-border shipments, or reseller obligations.

The bill uses Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act as the ban vehicle but does not amend Section 8 itself to reflect the addition, leaving the ban to interact with existing CPSC rulemaking timelines.
The 90-day effective date does not include a labeling or notice-to-retailers requirement to help retailers comply.
The bill excludes drugs, devices, cosmetics, and foods but does not address dual-use products where sodium nitrite is a preservative in one context and a stand-alone chemical in another.

added: New statutory banned-hazardous-product designation under Section 8 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2057) for consumer products containing 10% or more sodium nitrite by weight
